I’ve always liked the idea that a day can contain more than one weather. Not just rain or sun, but the weather of thoughts: a bright morning mind, a foggy afternoon, a windy little burst of anxiety at 3 p.m., and then the quiet clear sky that sometimes arrives without warning in the evening. We talk about moods as if they are failures to be managed, but maybe they are closer to seasons—temporary, patterned, and full of their own instructions.

A rainy day asks for different virtues than a sunny one. Rain teaches patience. Sunlight teaches attention. Wind teaches flexibility. Snow, if you get it, teaches silence. Even the unpleasant weather has a kind of pedagogy. It changes the shape of a day and makes us renegotiate our plans, our pace, our expectations. A person who can step outside and accept the weather is practicing a very small form of wisdom.

I think about trees often for this reason. They do not argue with the sky. They simply take what comes, turn it into growth if they can, and otherwise endure. There is something almost heroic in that, though heroism is not the right word. It is more like competence at being alive.

Maybe that is enough for a life: not constant brilliance, not perfect clarity, just a decent relationship with change. To greet the weather as it is, and to keep walking anyway.
